entries.0e6b75d560dc874aaa98a86e9c21ff4d5f6a5f4f: <div sID="gen18006" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="38" osisID="Jer.38" sID="Jer.38"/> <div eID="gen18006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18007" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18008" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, just as in the former, we have Jeremiah greatly debased under the frowns of the princes, and yet greatly honoured by the favour of the king. They used him as a criminal; he used him as a privy-counsellor. Here, I. Jeremiah for his faithfulness is put into the dungeon by the princes, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.1-Jer.38.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. At the intercession of Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, by special order from the king, he is taken up out of the dungeon and confined only to the court of the prison, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.7-Jer.38.13">ver. 7-13</reference>. III. He has a private conference with the king upon the present conjuncture of affairs, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.14-Jer.38.22">ver. 14-22</reference>. IV. Care is taken to keep that conference private, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.24-Jer.38.28">ver. 24-28</reference>.
entries.cbe18c80f23229f68d4511c20afba31f9762fbc0: <div eID="gen18008" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18007" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Jeremiah Put into the Dungeon; Ebed-melech's Care of Jeremiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 589.)</title> <div sID="gen18009" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then Shephatiah the son of Mattan, and Gedaliah the son of Pashur, and Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashur the son of Malchiah, heard the words that Jeremiah had spoken unto all the people, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , He that remaineth in this city shall die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence: but he that goeth forth to the Chaldeans shall live; for he shall have his life for a prey, and shall live. <hi type="super">3</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , This city shall surely be given into the hand of the king of Babylon's army, which shall take it. <hi type="super">4</hi> Therefore the princes said unto the king, We beseech thee, let this man be put to death: for thus he weakeneth the hands of the men of war that remain in this city, and the hands of all the people, in speaking such words unto them: for this man seeketh not the welfare of this people, but the hurt. <hi type="super">5</hi> Then Zedekiah the king said, Behold, he <hi type="italic">is</hi> in your hand: for the king <hi type="italic">is</hi> not <hi type="italic">he that</hi> can do <hi type="italic">any</hi> thing against you. <hi type="super">6</hi> Then took they Jeremiah, and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah the son of Hammelech, that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in the court of the prison: and they let down Jeremiah with cords. And in the dungeon <hi type="italic">there was</hi> no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire. <hi type="super">7</hi> Now when Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, one of the eunuchs which was in the king's house, heard that they had put Jeremiah in the dungeon; the king then sitting in the gate of Benjamin; <hi type="super">8</hi> Ebed-melech went forth out of the king's house, and spake to the king, saying, <hi type="super">9</hi> My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they have done to Jeremiah the prophet, whom they have cast into the dungeon; and he is like to die for hunger in the place where he is: for <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no more bread in the city. <hi type="super">10</hi> Then the king commanded Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, saying, Take from hence thirty men with thee, and take up Jeremiah the prophet out of the dungeon, before he die. <hi type="super">11</hi> So Ebed-melech took the men with him, and went into the house of the king under the treasury, and took thence old cast clouts and old rotten rags, and let them down by cords into the dungeon to <reference osisRef="Jer.12">Jeremiah.   12</reference> And Ebed-melech the Ethiopian said unto Jeremiah, Put now <hi type="italic">these</hi> old cast clouts and rotten rags under thine armholes under the cords. And Jeremiah did so. <hi type="super">13</hi> So they drew up Jeremiah with cords, and took him up out of the dungeon: and Jeremiah remained in the court of the prison. <div eID="gen18009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18010" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. Jeremiah persists in his plain preaching; what he had many a time said, he still says (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">This city shall be given into the hand of the king of Babylon;</hi> though it hold out long, it will taken at last. Nor would he have so often repeated this unwelcome message but that he could put them in a certain way, though not to save the city, yet to save themselves; so that every man might have his own life given him for a prey if he would be advised, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.2">v. 2</reference>. Let him not stay in the city, in hopes to defend that, for it will be to no purpose, but let him <hi type="italic">go forth to the Chaldeans,</hi> and throw himself upon their mercy, before things come to extremity, and then he <hi type="italic">shall live;</hi> they will not put him to the sword, but give him quarter (<hi type="italic">satis est prostrasse leoni—it suffices the lion to lay his antagonist prostrate</hi>) and he shall escape the <hi type="italic">famine and pestilence,</hi> which will be the death of multitudes within the city. Note, Those do better for themselves who patiently submit to the rebukes of Providence than those who contend with them. And, if we cannot have our liberty, we must reckon it a mercy to have our lives, and not foolishly throw them away upon a point of honour; they may be reserved for better times. 2. The princes persist in their malice against Jeremiah. He was faithful to his country and to his trust as a prophet, though he had suffered many a time for his faithfulness; and, though at this time he ate the king's bread, yet that did not stop his mouth. But his persecutors were still bitter against him, and complained that he abused the liberty he had of walking in the court of the prison; for, though he could not go to the temple to preach, yet he vented the same things in private conversation to those that came to visit him, and therefore (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.4">v. 4</reference>) they represented him to the king as a dangerous man, disaffected to his country and to the government he lived under: <hi type="italic">He seeks not the welfare of this people, but the hurt</hi>—an unjust insinuation, for no man had laid out himself more for the good of Jerusalem than he had done. They represent his preaching as having a bad tendency. The design of it was plainly to bring men to repent and turn to God, which would have been as much as any thing a strengthening to the hands both the soldiery and of the burghers, and yet they represented it <hi type="italic">as weakening their hands</hi> and discouraging them; and, if it did this, it was their own fault. Note, It is common for wicked people to look upon God's faithful ministers as their enemies, only because they show them what enemies they are to themselves while they continue impenitent. 3. Jeremiah hereupon, by the king's permission, is put into a dungeon, with a view to his destruction there. Zedekiah, though he felt a conviction that Jeremiah was a prophet, sent of God, had not courage to own it, but yielded to the violence of his persecutors (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">He is in your hand;</hi> and a worse sentence he could not have passed upon him. We found in Jehoiakim's reign that the princes were better affected to the prophet than the king was (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.25">ch. xxxvi. 25</reference>); but now they were more violent against him, a sign that they were ripening apace for ruin. Had it been in a cause that concerned his own honour or profit, he would have let them know that the king is he who can do what he pleases, whether they will or no; but in the cause of God and his prophet, which he was very cool in, he basely sneaks, and truckles to them: <hi type="italic">The king is not he that can do any thing against you.</hi> Note, Those will have a great deal to answer for who, though they have a secret kindness for good people, dare not own it in a time of need, nor will do what they might do to prevent mischief designed them. The princes, having this general warrant from the king, immediately put poor <hi type="italic">Jeremiah into the dungeon of Malchiah, that was in the court of the prison</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.6">v. 6</reference>), a deep dungeon, for they <hi type="italic">let</hi> him <hi type="italic">down</hi> into it <hi type="italic">with cords,</hi> and a dirty one, for <hi type="italic">there was no water</hi> in it, <hi type="italic">but mire;</hi> and he <hi type="italic">sunk in the mire, up to the neck,</hi> says Josephus. Those that put him here doubtless designed that he should die here, die for hunger, die for cold, and so die miserably, die obscurely, fearing, if they should put him to death openly, the people might be affected with what he would say and be incensed against them. Many of God's faithful witnesses have thus been privately made away, and starved to death, in prisons, whose blood will be brought to account in the day of discovery. We are not here told what Jeremiah did in this distress, but he tells us himself (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.55">Lam. iii. 55</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.57">57</reference>), <hi type="italic">I called upon thy name, O Lord! out of the low dungeon, and thou drewest near, saying, Fear not.</hi> 4. Application is made to the king by an honest courtier, <hi type="italic">Ebed-melech,</hi> one of the gentlemen of the bed-chamber, in behalf of the poor sufferer. Though the princes carried on the matter as privately as they could, yet it came to the ear of this good man, who probably sought opportunities to do good. It may be he came to the knowledge of it by hearing Jeremiah's moans out of the dungeon, for it was in the king's house, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.7">v. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Ebed-melech</hi> was an Ethiopian, a <hi type="italic">stranger to the commonwealth of Israel,</hi> and yet had in him more humanity, and more divinity too, than native Israelites had. Christ found more faith among Gentiles than among Jews. Ebed-melech lived in a wicked court and in a very corrupt degenerate age, and yet had a great sense both of equity and piety. God has his remnant in all places, among all sorts. There were <hi type="italic">saints</hi> even <hi type="italic">in Cæsar's household.</hi> The king was now <hi type="italic">sitting in the gate of Benjamin,</hi> to try causes and receive appeals and petitions, or perhaps holding a council of war there. Thither Ebed-melech went immediately to him, for the case would not admit delay; the prophet might have perished if he had trifled or put it off till he had an opportunity of speaking to the king in private. Not time must be lost when life is in danger, especially so valuable a life. He boldly asserts the Jeremiah had a great deal of wrong done him, and is not afraid to tell the king so, though they were princes that did it, though they were now present in court, and though they had the king's warrant for what they did. Whither should oppressed innocency flee for protection but to the throne, especially when great men are its oppressors? Ebed-melech appears truly brave in this matter. He does not mince the matter; though he had a place at court, which he would be in danger of losing for his plain dealing, yet he tells the king faithfully, let him take it as he will, <hi type="italic">These men have done ill in all that they have done to Jeremiah.</hi> They had dealt unjustly with him, for he had not deserved any punishment at all; and they had dealt barbarously with him, so as they used not to deal with the vilest malefactors. And they needed not to have put him to this miserable death; for, if they had let him alone where he was, he was <hi type="italic">likely to die for hunger in the place where he was,</hi> in the court of the prison to which he was confined, <hi type="italic">for there was not more bread in the city:</hi> the stores out of which he was to have his allowance (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.21">ch. xxxvii. 21</reference>) were in a manner spent. See how God can raise up friends for his people in distress where they little thought of them, and animate men for his service even beyond expectation. 5. Orders are immediately given for his release, and Ebed-melech takes care to see them executed. The king, who but now durst do nothing against the princes, had his heart wonderfully changed on a sudden, and will now have Jeremiah released in defiance of the princes, for therefore he orders no less than thirty men, and those of the lifeguard, to be employed in fetching him out of the dungeon, lest the princes should raise a party to oppose it, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.10">v. 10</reference>. Let this encourage us to appear boldly for God—we may succeed better that we could have thought, for <hi type="italic">the hearts of kings are in the hand of God.</hi> Ebed-melech gained his point, and soon brought Jeremiah the good news; and it is observable how particularly the manner of his drawing him out of the dungeon is related (for <hi type="italic">God is not unrighteous to forget</hi> any <hi type="italic">work or labour of love</hi> which is shown to his people or ministers, no, nor any circumstance of it, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.10">Heb. vi. 10</reference>); special notice is taken of his great tenderness in providing old soft rags for Jeremiah to put under his arm-holes, to keep the cords wherewith he was to be drawn up from hurting him, his arm-holes being probably galled by the cords wherewith he was let down. Nor did he throw the rags down to him, lest they should be lost in the mire, but carefully let them down, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.11-Jer.38.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. Note, Those that are in distress should not only be relieved, but relieved with compassion and marks of respect, all which shall be placed to account and abound to a good account in the day of recompence. See what a good use even old rotten rags may be put to, which therefore should not be made waste of, any more than broken meat: even in the king's house, and <hi type="italic">under the treasury</hi> too, these were carefully preserved for the use of the poor or sick. Jeremiah is brought up out of the dungeon, and is now where he was, <hi type="italic">in the court of the prison,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.38.13">v. 13</reference>. Perhaps Ebed-melech could have made interest with the king to get him his discharge thence also, now that he had the king's ear; but he though him safer and better provided for there than he would be any where else. God can, when he pleases, make a prison to become a refuge and hiding-place to his people in distress and danger.
entries.d82f019e25c9e377685464e43d8102d0101c2051: <div eID="gen18010" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Zedekiah's Conference with Jeremiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 589.)</title> <div sID="gen18011" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Then Zedekiah the king sent, and took Jeremiah the prophet unto him into the third entry that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and the king said unto Jeremiah, I will ask thee a thing; hide nothing from me. <hi type="super">15</hi> Then Jeremiah said unto Zedekiah, If I declare <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto thee, wilt thou not surely put me to death? and if I give thee counsel, wilt thou not hearken unto me? <hi type="super">16</hi> So Zedekiah the king sware secretly unto Jeremiah, saying, <hi type="italic">As</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth, that made us this soul, I will not put thee to death, neither will I give thee into the hand of these men that seek thy life. <hi type="super">17</hi> Then said Jeremiah unto Zedekiah, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the God of hosts, the God of Israel; If thou wilt assuredly go forth unto the king of Babylon's princes, then thy soul shall live, and this city shall not be burned with fire; and thou shalt live, and thine house: <hi type="super">18</hi> But if thou wilt not go forth to the king of Babylon's princes, then shall this city be given into the hand of the Chaldeans, and they shall burn it with fire, and thou shalt not escape out of their hand. <hi type="super">19</hi> And Zedekiah the king said unto Jeremiah, I am afraid of the Jews that are fallen to the Chaldeans, lest they deliver me into their hand, and they mock me. <hi type="super">20</hi> But Jeremiah said, They shall not deliver <hi type="italic">thee.</hi> Obey, I beseech thee, the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , which I speak unto thee: so it shall be well unto thee, and thy soul shall live. <hi type="super">21</hi> But if thou refuse to go forth, this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the word that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath shewed me: <hi type="super">22</hi> And, behold, all the women that are left in the king of Judah's house <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> brought forth to the king of Babylon's princes, and those <hi type="italic">women</hi> shall say, Thy friends have set thee on, and have prevailed against thee: thy feet are sunk in the mire, <hi type="italic">and</hi> they are turned away back. <hi type="super">23</hi> So they shall bring out all thy wives and thy children to the Chaldeans: and thou shalt not escape out of their hand, but shalt be taken by the hand of the king of Babylon: and thou shalt cause this city to be burned with fire. <hi type="super">24</hi> Then said Zedekiah unto Jeremiah, Let no man know of these words, and thou shalt not die. <hi type="super">25</hi> But if the princes hear that I have talked with thee, and they come unto thee, and say unto thee, Declare unto us now what thou hast said unto the king, hide it not from us, and we will not put thee to death; also what the king said unto thee: <hi type="super">26</hi> Then thou shalt say unto them, I presented my supplication before the king, that he would not cause me to return to Jonathan's house, to die there. <hi type="super">27</hi> Then came all the princes unto Jeremiah, and asked him: and he told them according to all these words that the king had commanded. So they left off speaking with him; for the matter was not perceived. <hi type="super">28</hi> So Jeremiah abode in the court of the prison until the day that Jerusalem was taken: and he was <hi type="italic">there</hi> when Jerusalem was taken. <div eID="gen18011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18012" type="x-p"/> In the foregoing chapter we had the king in close conference with Jeremiah, and here again, though (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.5">v. 5</reference>) he had given him up into the hands of his enemies; such a struggle there was in the breast of this unhappy prince between his convictions and his corruptions. Observe, <div eID="gen18012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18013" type="x-p"/> I. The honour that Zedekiah did to the prophet. When he was newly fetched out of the dungeon he sent for him to advise with him privately. He met him in <hi type="italic">the third entry,</hi> or (as the margin reads it) <hi type="italic">the principal entry,</hi> that <hi type="italic">is in,</hi> or leads towards, or adjoins to, <hi type="italic">the house of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.38.14">v. 14</reference>. In appointing this place of interview with the prophet perhaps he intended to show a respect and reverence for <hi type="italic">the house of God,</hi> which was proper enough now that he was desiring to hear <hi type="italic">the word of God.</hi> Zedekiah would ask <hi type="italic">Jeremiah a thing;</hi> it should rather be rendered, <hi type="italic">a word.</hi> "I am here asking thee for <hi type="italic">a word of prediction,</hi> of counsel, of comfort, <hi type="italic">a word from the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.37.17">ch. xxxvii. 17</reference>. Whatever word thou has for me <hi type="italic">hide it not from me;</hi> let me know the worst." He had been told plainly what things would come to in the foregoing chapter, but, like Balaam, he asks again, in hopes to get a more pleasing answer, as if God, who is <hi type="italic">in one mind,</hi> were altogether such a one as himself, who was in many minds. <div eID="gen18013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18014" type="x-p"/> II. The bargain that Jeremiah made with him before he would give him his advice, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.15">v. 15</reference>. He would stipulate, 1. For his own safety. Zedekiah would have him deal faithfully with him: "And if I do," says Jeremiah, "<hi type="italic">wilt thou not put me to death?</hi> I am afraid <hi type="italic">thou wilt</hi>" (so some take it); "what else can I expect when thou art led blindfold by the princes?" Not that Jeremiah was backward to seal the doctrine he preached with his blood, when he was called to do so; but, in doing our duty, we ought to use all lawful means for our own preservation; even the apostles of Christ did so. 2. He would answer for the success of his advice, being no less concerned for Zedekiah's welfare than for his own. He is willing to give him wholesome advice, and does not upbraid him with his unkindness in suffering him to be put into the dungeon, nor bid him go and consult with his princes, whose judgments he had such a value for. Ministers must with meekness instruct even those that oppose themselves, and render good for evil. He is desirous that he should <hi type="italic">hear counsel and receive instruction: "Wilt thou not hearken unto me?</hi> Surely thou wilt; I am in hopes to find thee pliable at last, and now <hi type="italic">in this thy day</hi> willing to know <hi type="italic">the things that belong to thy peace.</hi>" Note, Then, and then only, there is hope of sinners, when they are willing to hearken to good counsel. Some read it as spoken despairingly: "<hi type="italic">If I give thee counsel, thou wilt not hearken unto me;</hi> I have reason to fear thou wilt not, and then I might as well keep my counsel to myself." Note, Ministers have little heart to speak to those who have long and often turned a deaf ear to them. Now, as to this latter concern of Jeremiah's, Zedekiah makes him no answer, will not promise to hearken to his advice: though he desires to know what is the mind of God, yet he will reserve himself a liberty, when he does know it, to do as he thinks fit; as if it were the prerogative of a prince not to have his ruin prevented by good counsel. But, as to the prophet's safety, he promises him, upon the word of a king, and confirms his promise with an oath, that, whatever he should say to him, no advantage should be taken against him for it: <hi type="italic">I will neither put thee to death nor deliver thee into the hands of those that will,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.38.16">v. 16</reference>. This, he thought, was a mighty favour, and yet Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar, when Daniel read their doom, not only protected him, but preferred and rewarded him, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.48">Dan. ii. 48</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.38.29">v. 29</reference>. Zedekiah's oath on this occasion is solemn, and very observable: "<hi type="italic">As the Lord liveth, who made us this soul,</hi> who gave me my life and thee thine, I dare not take away thy life unjustly, knowing that then I should forfeit my own to him that is the Lord of life." Note, God is the Father of spirits; souls are his workmanship, and they are more <hi type="italic">fearfully and wonderfully made</hi> than bodies are. The soul both of the greatest prince and of the poorest prisoner is of God's making. <hi type="italic">He fashioneth their hearts</hi> alike easily. In all our appeals to God, and in all our dealings both with ourselves and others, we ought to consider this, that <hi type="italic">the living God made us these souls.</hi> <div eID="gen18014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18015" type="x-p"/> III. The good advice that Jeremiah gave him, with good reasons why he should take it, not from any prudence or politics of his own, but in the <hi type="italic">name of the Lord, the God of hosts</hi> and <hi type="italic">God of Israel.</hi> Not as a statesman, but as a prophet, he advises him by all means to surrender himself and his city <hi type="italic">to the king of Babylon's princes: "Go forth to them,</hi> and make the best terms thou canst with them," <reference osisRef="Jer.38.17">v. 17</reference>. This was the advice he had given to the people (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.2">v. 2</reference>, and before, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.9">ch. xxi. 9</reference>), to submit to divine judgments, and not think of contending with them. Note, In dealing with God, that which is good counsel to the meanest is so to the greatest, for <hi type="italic">there is no respect of persons</hi> with him. To persuade him to take this counsel, he sets before him good and evil, life and death. 1. If he will tamely yield, he shall save his children from the sword and Jerusalem from the flames. The white flag is yet hung out; if he will but acknowledge God's justice, he shall experience his mercy: <hi type="italic">The city shall not be burnt,</hi> and <hi type="italic">thou shalt live and thy house.</hi> But, 2. If he will obstinately stand it out, it will be the ruin both of his house and Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.18">v. 18</reference>); for when God judges he will overcome. This is the case of sinners with God; let them humbly submit to his grace and government and they shall live; let them <hi type="italic">take hold on his strength, that they may make peace, and they shall make peace;</hi> but, if they harden their hearts against his proposals, it will certainly be to their destruction: they must either bend or break. <div eID="gen18015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18016" type="x-p"/> IV. The objection which Zedekiah made against the prophet's advice, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.19">v. 19</reference>. Jeremiah spoke to him by prophecy, in the name of God, and therefore if he had had a due regard to the divine authority, wisdom, and goodness, as soon as he understood what the mind of God was he would immediately have acquiesced in it and resolved to observe it, without disputing; but, as if it had been the dictate only of Jeremiah's prudence, he advances against it some prudential considerations of his own: but human wisdom is folly when it contradicts the divine counsel. All he suggests is, "<hi type="italic">I am afraid,</hi> not of the Chaldeans; their princes are men of honour, but of the Jews, that have already gone over to the Chaldeans; when they see <hi type="italic">me</hi> follow them, and who had so much opposed their going, they will laugh at me, and say, <hi type="italic">Hast thou also become weak as water?</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.14.10">Isa. xiv. 10</reference>. Now, 1. It was not at all likely that he should be thus exposed and ridiculed, that the Chaldeans should so far gratify the Jews, or trample upon him, as to deliver him into their hands; nor that the Jews, who were themselves captives, should be in such a gay humour as to make a jest of the misery of their prince. Note, We often frighten ourselves from our duty by foolish, causeless, groundless, fears, that are merely the creatures of our own fancy and imagination. 2. If he should be taunted at a little by the Jews, could he not despise it and make light of it? What harm would it do him? Note, Those have very weak and fretful spirits indeed that cannot bear to be laughed at for that which is both their duty and their interest. 3. Though it had been really the greatest personal mischief that he could imagine it to be, yet he ought to have ventured it, in obedience to God, and for the preservation of his family and city. He thought it would be looked upon as a piece of cowardice to surrender; whereas it would be really an instance of true courage cheerfully to bear a less evil, the mocking of the Jews, for the avoiding of a greater, the ruin of his family and kingdom. <div eID="gen18016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18017" type="x-p"/> V. The pressing importunity with which Jeremiah followed the advice he had given the king. He assures him that, if he would comply with the will of God herein, the thing he feared should not come upon him (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall not deliver thee up,</hi> but treat thee as becomes thy character. He begs of him, after all the foolish games he had played, to manage wisely the last stake, and now at length to do well for himself: <hi type="italic">Obey, I beseech thee, the voice of the Lord,</hi> because it is his voice, so it <hi type="italic">shall be well unto thee.</hi> But he tells him what would be the consequence if he would not obey. 1. He himself would <hi type="italic">fall into the hands of the Chaldeans,</hi> as implacable enemies, whom he might now make his friends by throwing himself into their hands. If he must fall, he should contrive how to fall easily: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt not escape,</hi> as thou hopest to do," <reference osisRef="Jer.38.23">v. 23</reference>. 2. He would himself be chargeable with the destruction of Jerusalem, which he pretended a concern for the preservation of: <hi type="italic">"Thou shalt cause this city to be burnt with fire,</hi> for by a little submission and self-denial thou mightest have prevented it." Thus subjects often suffer for the pride and wilfulness of their rulers, who should be their protectors, but prove their destroyers. 3. Whereas he causelessly feared an unjust reproach for surrendering, he should certainly fall under a just reproach for standing it out, and that from women too, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.22">v. 22</reference>. The court ladies who were left when Jehoiakim and Jeconiah were carried away will now at length fall into the hands of the enemy, and they shall say, "<hi type="italic">The men of thy peace,</hi> whom thou didst consult with and confide in, and who promised thee peace if thou wouldst be ruled by them, have <hi type="italic">set thee on,</hi> have encouraged thee to be bold and brace and hold out to the last extremity; and see what comes of it? They, by prevailing upon thee, have <hi type="italic">prevailed against thee,</hi> and thou findest those thy real enemies that would be thought thy only friends. <hi type="italic">Now thy feet are sunk in the mire,</hi> thou art embarrassed, and hast noway to help thyself; thy feet cannot get forward, but are <hi type="italic">turned away back.</hi>" Thus will Zedekiah be bantered by the women, when all his wives and children shall be made a prey to the conquerors, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.23">v. 23</reference>. Note, What we seek to avoid by sin will be justly brought upon us by the righteousness of God. And those that decline the way of duty for fear of reproach will certainly meet with much greater reproach in the way of disobedience. <hi type="italic">The fear of the wicked, it shall come upon him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.24">Prov. x. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen18017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18018" type="x-p"/> VI. The care which Zedekiah took to keep this conference private (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let no man know of these words.</hi> he does not at all incline to take God's counsel, nor so much as promise to consider of it; for so obstinate has he been to the calls of God, and so wilful in the ways of sin, that though he has good counsel given him he seems to be given up to walk in his own counsels. He has nothing to object against Jeremiah's advice, and yet he will not follow it. Many hear God's words, but will not do them. 1. Jeremiah is charged to let no man know of what had passed between the king and him. Zedekiah is concerned to keep it private, not so much for Jeremiah's safety (for he knew the princes could do him no hurt without his permission), but for his own reputation. Note, Many have really a better affection to good men and good things than they are willing to own. God's prophets are manifest in their consciences (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.11">2 Cor. v. 11</reference>), but they care not for manifesting that to the world; they would rather do them a kindness than have it known that they do: such, it is to be feared, <hi type="italic">love the praise of men more than the praise of God.</hi> 2. He is instructed what to say to the princes if they should examine him about it. He must tell them that he was petitioning the king not to remand him back to <hi type="italic">the house of Jonathan the scribe</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.25-Jer.38.26">v. 25, 26</reference>), and he did tell them so (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.27">v. 27</reference>), and no doubt it was true: he would not let slip so fair an opportunity of engaging the king's favour; so that this was no lie or equivocation, but a part of the truth, which it was lawful for him to put them off with when he was under no obligation at all to tell them the whole truth. Note, Though we must be harmless as doves, so as never to tell a wilful lie, yet we must be wise as serpents, so as not needlessly to expose ourselves to danger by telling all we know.  <chapter eID="Jer.38"/> <div eID="gen18018" type="x-p"/>

entries.faf91615ff759791549a607090961e170a58e216: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10428"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 38</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.38.1-Jer.38.28">Jr 38:1-28</reference>. Jeremiah Predicts the Capture of Jerusalem, for Which He Is Cast into a Dungeon, but Is Transferred to the Prison Court on the Intercession of Ebed-melech, and Has a Secret Interview with Zedekiah.</title> <div sID="gen18596" type="x-p"/> All this was subsequent to his imprisonment in Jonathan's house, and his release on his interview with Zedekiah. The latter occurred before the return of the Chaldeans to the siege; the similar events in this chapter occurred after it.<div eID="gen18596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18597" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10428"/><hi type="bold">1. Jucal--</hi>Jehucal (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.3">Jr 37:3</reference>).<div eID="gen18597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18598" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Pashur--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jr 21:1</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.21.9">Jr 21:9</reference> with <reference osisRef="Jer.38.2">Jr 38:2</reference>). The deputation in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jr 21:1</reference>, to whom Jeremiah gave this reply, if not identical with the hearers of Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.1">Jr 38:1</reference>), must have been sent just before the latter "heard" him speaking the same words. Zephaniah is not mentioned here as in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jr 21:1</reference>, but is so in <reference osisRef="Jer.37.3">Jr 37:3</reference>. Jucal is mentioned here and in the previous deputation (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.3">Jr 37:3</reference>), but not in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jr 21:1</reference>. Shephatiah and Gedaliah here do not occur either in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jr 21:1</reference> or <reference osisRef="Jer.37.3">Jr 37:3</reference>. The identity of his words in both cases is natural, when uttered, at a very short interval, and one of the hearers (Pashur) being present on both occasions.<div eID="gen18598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18599" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto all the people--</hi>They had free access to him in the court of the prison (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.12">Jr 32:12</reference>). <div eID="gen18599" type="x-p"/>
entries.bcc309334a150b3f876243d3fadbb9f62810d215: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10429"/><div sID="gen18600" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10429"/><hi type="bold">2. life ... a prey--</hi>He shall escape with his life; though losing all else in a shipwreck, he shall carry off his life as his gain, saved by his going over to the Chaldeans. (See on <reference osisRef="Jer.21.9">Jr 21:9</reference>). <div eID="gen18600" type="x-p"/>
entries.b4899e1b43daf4d070d3e328a2251123a859552a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10430"/><div sID="gen18601" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10430"/>4. Had Jeremiah not had a divine commission, he might justly have been accused of treason; but having one, which made the result of the siege certain, he acted humanely as interpreter of God's will under the theocracy, in advising surrender (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.26.11">Jr 26:11</reference>). <div eID="gen18601" type="x-p"/>
entries.a606a58894029c7fba7d380ba4f4d9c12025dae2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10431"/><div sID="gen18602" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10431"/><hi type="bold">5. the king is not he--</hi>Zedekiah was a weak prince, and now in his straits afraid to oppose his princes. He hides his dislike of their overweening power, which prevented him shielding Jeremiah as he would have wished, under complimentary speeches. "It is not right that the king should deny aught to such faithful and wise statesmen"; the king is not such a one as to deny you your wishes [Jerome]. <div eID="gen18602" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a955b946c3ef8dbffa08e71c6047648836b4ac4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10432"/><div sID="gen18603" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10432"/><hi type="bold">6. dungeon--</hi>literally, the "cistern." It was not a subterranean prison as that in Jonathan's house (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.15">Jr 37:15</reference>), but a pit or cistern, which had been full of water, but was emptied of it during the siege, so that only "mire" remained. Such empty cisterns were often used as prisons (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.11">Zec 9:11</reference>); the depth forbade hope of escape.<div eID="gen18603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18604" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hammelech--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.36.26">Jr 36:26</reference>). His son followed in the father's steps, a ready tool for evil.<div eID="gen18604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18605" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sunk in the mire--</hi>Jeremiah herein was a type of Messiah (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.2">Psa 69:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.14">14</reference>). "I sink in deep mire," &c. <div eID="gen18605" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd3af70efd78116d917bb3a9659d1e6d61e7cf30: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10433"/><div sID="gen18606" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10433"/><hi type="bold">7. Ebed-melech--</hi>The Hebrew designation given this Ethiopian, meaning "king's servant." Already, even at this early time, God wished to show what good reason there was for calling the Gentiles to salvation. An Ethiopian stranger saves the prophet whom his own countrymen, the Jews, tried to destroy. So the Gentiles believed in Christ whom the Jews crucified, and Ethiopians were among the earliest converts (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.10">Ac 2:10</reference>, 41; 8:27-39). Ebed-melech probably was keeper of the royal harem, and so had private access to the king. The eunuchs over harems in the present day are mostly from Nubia or Abyssinia. <div eID="gen18606" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd4bf1f9dfcb2645a3b03d934cf728da4538163d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10434"/><div sID="gen18607" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10434"/><hi type="bold">8. went forth ... and spake--</hi>not privately, but in public; a proof of fearless magnanimity. <div eID="gen18607" type="x-p"/>
entries.26ea00322a6a79da77622331eea125ee6bf1ff50: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10435"/><div sID="gen18608" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10435"/><hi type="bold">9. die for hunger in the place where he is; for ... no ... bread in ... city--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.37.21">Jr 37:21</reference>). He had heretofore got a piece of bread supplied to him. "Seeing that there is the utmost want of bread in the city, so that even if he were at large, there could no more be regularly supplied to him, much less now in a place where none remember or pity him, so that he is likely to die for hunger." "No more bread," that is, no more left of the public store in the city (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.21">Jr 37:21</reference>); or, all but no bread left anywhere [Maurer]. <div eID="gen18608" type="x-p"/>
entries.7bc844a5a41ad18add4dcaaaf5272e2c742839ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10436"/><div sID="gen18609" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10436"/><hi type="bold">10. with thee--</hi>Hebrew, "in thine hand," that is, at "thy disposal" (<reference osisRef="1Sam.16.2">1Sa 16:2</reference>). "From hence," that is, from the gate of Benjamin where the king was sitting (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.7">Jr 38:7</reference>).<div eID="gen18609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18610" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thirty men--</hi>not merely to draw up Jeremiah, but to guard Ebed-melech against any opposition on the part of the princes (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.1-Jer.38.4">Jr 38:1-4</reference>), in executing the king's command. Ebed-melech was rewarded for his faith, love, and courage, exhibited at a time when he might well fear the wrath of the princes, to which even the king had to yield (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.16-Jer.39.18">Jr 39:16-18</reference>). <div eID="gen18610" type="x-p"/>
entries.a0c73279ec1ecf6566b45a7171bfa597dca4117b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10437"/><div sID="gen18611" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10437"/><hi type="bold">11. cast clouts--</hi>"torn clothes" [Henderson].<div eID="gen18611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18612" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rotten rags--</hi>"worn-out garments." God can make the meanest things His instruments of goodness to His people (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.27-1Cor.1.29">1Co 1:27-29</reference>).<div eID="gen18612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18613" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">under ... armholes--</hi>"under the joints of thine hands," that is, where the fingers join the hand, the clothes being in order that the hands should not be cut by the cords [Maurer]. <div eID="gen18613" type="x-p"/>
entries.1afa9a064e46fa0ba5330859f3eb707cd8879e8d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10438"/><div sID="gen18614" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10438"/><hi type="bold">13. court of ... prison--</hi>Ebed-melech prudently put him there to be out of the way of his enemies. <div eID="gen18614" type="x-p"/>
entries.1670fd32d9803b01a3aa1f4b6f73f1b36aeed792: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10439"/><div sID="gen18615" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10439"/><hi type="bold">14. third entry--</hi>The Hebrews in determining the position of places faced the east, which they termed "that which is in front"; the south was thus called "that which is on the right hand"; the north, "that which is on the left hand"; the west, "that which is behind." So beginning with the east they might term it the first or principal entry; the south the second entry; the north the "third entry" of the outer or inner court [Maurer]. The third gate of the temple facing the palace; for through it the entrance lay from the palace into the temple (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.5">1Ki 10:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.12">12</reference>). It was westward (<reference osisRef="1Chr.26.16">1Ch 26:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.26.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.11">2Ch 9:11</reference>) [Grotius]. But in the future temple it is eastward (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.1">Eze 46:1</reference>, 2, 8). <div eID="gen18615" type="x-p"/>
entries.e6d2b43d90a072a53520ecc5cbbf00848455f590: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10440"/><div sID="gen18616" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10440"/><hi type="bold">15. wilt thou not hearken unto me--</hi>Zedekiah does not answer this last query; the former one he replies to in <reference osisRef="Jer.38.16">Jr 38:16</reference>. Rather translate, "Thou wilt not hearken to me." Jeremiah judges so from the past conduct of the king. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.38.17">Jr 38:17</reference> with <reference osisRef="Jer.38.19">Jr 38:19</reference>. <div eID="gen18616" type="x-p"/>
entries.3dc59e46c3d0864c6e7426a5e8f596c58c7822f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10441"/><div sID="gen18617" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10441"/><hi type="bold">16. Lord ... made us this soul--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.57.16">Is 57:16</reference>). Implying, "may my life (soul) be forfeited if I deceive thee" [Calvin]. <div eID="gen18617" type="x-p"/>
entries.7425c12f2af0fbd21e6a3c257ed908704499f1f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10442"/><div sID="gen18618" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10442"/><hi type="bold">17. princes--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.39.3">Jr 39:3</reference>). He does not say "to the king himself," for he was at Riblah, in Hamath (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.5">Jr 39:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.6">2Ki 25:6</reference>). "If thou go forth" (namely, to surrender; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.12">2Ki 24:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.36.16">Is 36:16</reference>), God foreknows future conditional contingencies, and ordains not only the end, but also the means to the end. <div eID="gen18618" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a3ac7ddbc0ce3a237fec3158b1f3c44acfd3120: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10443"/><div sID="gen18619" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10443"/><hi type="bold">19. afraid of the Jews--</hi>more than of God (<reference osisRef="Prov.29.25">Pr 29:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.9.22">Joh 9:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.43">12:43</reference>).<div eID="gen18619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18620" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mock me--</hi>treat me injuriously (<reference osisRef="1Sam.31.4">1Sa 31:4</reference>). <div eID="gen18620" type="x-p"/>
entries.d6e6614eddfcaa074800ebb55d4d02ef6e196b4a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10444"/><div sID="gen18621" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10444"/><hi type="bold">22. women--</hi>The very evil which Zedekiah wished to escape by disobeying the command to go forth shall befall him in its worst form thereby. Not merely the Jewish deserters shall "mock" him (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.19">Jr 38:19</reference>), but the very "women" of his own palace and harem, to gratify their new lords, will taunt him. A noble king in sooth, to suffer thyself to be so imposed on!<div eID="gen18621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18622" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thy friends--</hi>Hebrew, "men of thy peace" (see <reference osisRef="Jer.20.10">Jr 20:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.41.9">Psa 41:9</reference>, Margin). The king's ministers and the false prophets who misled him.<div eID="gen18622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18623" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sunk in ... mire--</hi>proverbial for, Thou art involved by "thy friends'" counsels in inextricable difficulties. The phrase perhaps alludes to <reference osisRef="Jer.38.6">Jr 38:6</reference>; a just retribution for the treatment of Jeremiah, who literally "sank in the mire."<div eID="gen18623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18624" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they are turned ... back--</hi>Having involved thee in the calamity, they themselves shall provide for their own safety by deserting to the Chaldeans (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.19">Jr 38:19</reference>). <div eID="gen18624" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b649813a77954f199ab54f18fc5849e0cea1f9b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10445"/><div sID="gen18625" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10445"/><hi type="bold">23. children--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.39.6">Jr 39:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.41.10">41:10</reference>). "wives ... children ... thou"; an ascending climax. <div eID="gen18625" type="x-p"/>
entries.edfb616f9f4c93bce811133c2e51e2155b60bfc1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10446"/><div sID="gen18626" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10446"/><hi type="bold">24. Let no man know--</hi>If thou wilt not tell this to the people, I will engage thy safety. <div eID="gen18626" type="x-p"/>
entries.9e82ca67cd46fe70d834af82d471b041367f0ce1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10447"/><div sID="gen18627" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10447"/>25. Kings are often such only in title; they are really under the power of their subjects. <div eID="gen18627" type="x-p"/>
entries.23d350190e99f58fb9e315d65d4fcb4674e9de88: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10448"/><div sID="gen18628" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10448"/><hi type="bold">26. presented--</hi>literally, "made my supplication to fall"; implying supplication with humble prostration (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.36.7">Jr 36:7</reference>).<div eID="gen18628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18629" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jonathan's house--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.37.15">Jr 37:15</reference>), different from Malchiah's dungeon (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.6">Jr 38:6</reference>). This statement was true, though not the whole truth; the princes had no right to the information; no sanction is given by Scripture here to Jeremiah's representation of this being the cause of his having come to the king. Fear drove him to it. Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.20.2">Ge 20:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.20.12">12</reference>; on the other hand, <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.2">1Sa 16:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.5">5</reference>.<div eID="gen18629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18630" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">left off speaking with--</hi>Hebrew, "were silent from him," that is, withdrawing from him they left him quiet (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.8">1Sa 7:8</reference>, Margin). <div eID="gen18630" type="x-p"/>
entries.bbd68228ffa016865ae82933fda19b8c148e78da: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10449"/><div sID="gen18631" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10449"/><hi type="bold">28. he was there when Jerusalem was taken--</hi>These words are made the beginning of the thirty-ninth chapter by many; but the accents and sense support English Version. <chapter eID="Jer.38"/>

entries.e97626be0ab495e13229d556f116310b2128c5d0: <div eID="gen30362" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen30363" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30364" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30364" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30363" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30365" type="x-p"/> The princes of Judah, taking offense at Jeremiah on account of his predicting the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple by the Chaldeans, cause him to be cast into a deep and miry dungeon, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.1-Jer.38.6">Jer 38:1-6</reference>. Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian, gets the king's permission to take him out, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.7-Jer.38.13">Jer 38:7-13</reference>. Jeremiah advises the king, who consulted him privately, to surrender to the Chaldeans, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.14-Jer.38.23">Jer 38:14-23</reference>. The king promises the prophet that he will not put him to death, and requires him not to reveal what had passed to the princes; to whom he accordingly gives an evasive answer, telling them only so much of the conference as related to his request for his life, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.24-Jer.38.28">Jer 38:24-28</reference>. <div eID="gen30365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30366" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen30366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30367" type="x-p"/> Then Shephatiah - This was the faction - what Dahler terms the Antitheocratic faction - who were enemies to Jeremiah, and sought his life.
entries.1749286c5b5e94016d679dccfa3a54f6bf90eef6: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen30367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30368" type="x-p"/> This city shall surely be given - This was a testimony that be constantly bore: he had the authority of God for it. He knew it was true, and he never wavered nor equivocated.
entries.b04f6456a8513be7e4853273121ae7b4ff795a77: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen30368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30369" type="x-p"/> Let this man be put to death - And they gave their reasons plain enough: but the proof was wanting.
entries.9ecdca0c2de2954f267588c3f58c36a05af5a43d: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen30369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30370" type="x-p"/> He is in your hand - Ye have power to do as you please; I must act by your counsel. Poor weak prince! you respect the prophet, you fear the cabal, and you sacrifice an innocent man to your own weakness and their malice!
entries.9b1e05b7c5ecd27b09ac2092b4a613746e6d8c2a: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen30370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30371" type="x-p"/> So Jeremiah sunk in the mire - Their obvious design was, that he might be stifled in that place.
entries.5f76fa7cfaf794ffb28bfa5a1957b83463e5ee03: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen30371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30372" type="x-p"/> Ebed-melech - The servant of the king one of the eunuchs who belonged to the palace. Perhaps it should be read, "Now, a servant of the king, a Cushite, one of the eunuchs," etc. <div eID="gen30372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30373" type="x-p"/> The king then sitting in the gate of Benjamin - To give audience, and to administer justice. We have often seen that the gates of cities were the places of public judicature.
entries.1e081cddd9d4da7c52a1d4e9f7bb5938209a4388: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen30373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30374" type="x-p"/> My lord the king, these men have done evil - He must have been much in the king's confidence, and a humane and noble spirited man, thus to have raised his voice against the powerful cabal already mentioned. <div eID="gen30374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30375" type="x-p"/> There is no more bread in the city - They had defended it to the last extremity; and it appears that bread had been afforded to the prophet according to the king's commandment, as long as there was any remaining. See <reference osisRef="Jer.36.21">Jer 36:21</reference>.
entries.e3773e3931a6ec6419f017185ceaa67dafa1f077: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen30375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30376" type="x-p"/> Take from hence thirty men - The king was determined that he should be rescued by force, if the princes opposed.
entries.ab0493dbf84cd684d3e4ecbe15c3d83a39cded24: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen30376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30377" type="x-p"/> Went into the house of the king - and took thence - The eastern kings had their wardrobes always well furnished; as garments were a usual present to ambassadors, etc. I cannot think that, in the proper acceptation of the words, these were in any part of the king's house. <div eID="gen30377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30378" type="x-p"/> Old cast clouts, and old rotten rags - The fact seems to be this: there were several garments that had been used, and would not be used again; and there were others which, through continuing long there, had by insects, etc., been rendered useless. These he took, tied to the cord, let down to the prophet, that he might roll them round the ropes, and place them under his arm-pits, so that in being hauled up he might not suffer injury from the ropes, which in this case must sustain the whole weight of his body.
entries.c314b324024742f4eabb14c140c5c3fc392b0be8: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen30378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30379" type="x-p"/> Into the third entry - A place to enter which two others must be passed through.
entries.561dd6f79b355dfd6fe85d22d83bb3cbe952ad10: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen30379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30380" type="x-p"/> As the Lord liveth, that made us this soul - He is the living God, and he is the Author of that life which each of us possesses; and as sure as he lives, and we live by him, I will not put thee to death, nor give thee into the hands of those men who seek thy life. A very solemn oath; and the first instance on record of the profane custom of swearing by the soul.
entries.a6bef92e0e3ccb196db1e26a47d7788d1a38e7be: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen30380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30381" type="x-p"/> Wilt assuredly go - On the king's obedience to the advice of the prophet the safety of the city depended. <div eID="gen30381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30382" type="x-p"/> Unto the king of Babylon's princes - The generals of the army then returning to the siege from the defeat of the Egyptians; for Nebuchadnezzar himself was then at Riblah, in Syria, <reference osisRef="Jer.39.5">Jer 39:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.39.6">Jer 39:6</reference>.
entries.8c4af82d01aa0f78b683ce1327bb21d1fe2d7dd0: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen30382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30383" type="x-p"/> They mock me - Insult me, and exhibit me in triumph.
entries.37f2674273b2c91cebc8b95d3960c06f8112c412: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen30383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30384" type="x-p"/> All the women - brought forth - I think this place speaks of a kind of defection among the women of the harem; many of whom had already gone forth privately to the principal officers of the Chaldean army, and made the report mentioned in the end of this verse. These were the concubines or women of the second rank.
entries.1b5e1e3688867f78abd337df85972e796780aaab: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen30384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30385" type="x-p"/> They shall bring out all thy wives and thy children - These were the women of the first rank, by whom the king had children. These had no temptation to go out to the Chaldeans, nor would they have been made welcome; but the others being young, and without children, would be well received by the Chaldean princes.
entries.4da6e8446d5c34bc1ac533fd6b0c69c3f52554cf: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen30385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30386" type="x-p"/> I presented my supplication - This was telling the truth, and nothing but the truth, but not the whole truth. The king did not wish him to defile his conscience, nor did he propose any thing that was not consistent with the truth.
entries.b91395a90752529a29d0dfde5c9f00cc6ac97290: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen30386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30387" type="x-p"/> The matter was not perceived - They did not question him farther; and the king's commandment to remove him from the house of Jonathan being well known, they took for granted that they had all the information that they sought. And he was most certainly not obliged to relate any thing that might embroil this weak king with his factious but powerful princes, or affect his own life. He related simply what was necessary, and no more.  <chapter eID="Jer.38"/> <div eID="gen30387" type="x-p"/>

entries.03aff0b78517f5db28ca1fd7e18cb35fba788004: <reference osisRef="Jer.38.1-Jer.38.4">Jer 38:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen14294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14295" type="x-p"/> Jeremiah is cast into a miry pit, but drawn out again by Ebedmelech the Cushite. <reference osisRef="Jer.38.1">Jer 38:1</reference>-6. Being confined in the court of the guard attached to the royal palace, Jeremiah had opportunities of conversing with the soldiers stationed there and the people of Judah who came thither (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.38.1">Jer 38:1</reference> with <reference osisRef="Jer.32.8">Jer 32:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.12">Jer 32:12</reference>), and of declaring, in opposition to them, his conviction (which he had indeed expressed from the beginning of the siege) that all resistance to the Chaldeans would be fruitless, and only bring destruction (cf. Jer 21:9.). On this account, the princes who were of a hostile disposition towards him were so embittered, that they resolved on his death, and obtain from the king permission to cast him into a deep pit with mire at the bottom. In v. 1 four of these princes are named, two of whom, Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashur the son of Malchiah, are known, from <reference osisRef="Jer.37.3">Jer 37:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jer 21:1</reference>, as confidants of the king; the other two, Shephatiah the son of Mattan, and Gedaliah the son of Pashur, are not mentioned elsewhere. Gedaliah was probably a son of the Pashur who had once put Jeremiah in the stocks (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.1-Jer.20.2">Jer 20:1-2</reference>). The words of the prophet, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.2">Jer 38:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.3">Jer 38:3</reference>, are substantially the same as he had already uttered at the beginning of the siege, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.9">Jer 21:9</reference> (יחיה as in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.9">Jer 21:9</reference>). Jer 38:4. The princes said to the king, "Let this man, we beseech thee, be put to death for the construction, see on <reference osisRef="Jer.35.14">Jer 35:14</reference>; for therefore i.e., because no one puts him out of existence - על־כּן as in <reference osisRef="Jer.29.28">Jer 29:28</reference> he weakens the hands of the men of war who remain in this city, and the hands of all the people, by speaking words like these to them; for this man does not seek the welfare of this people, but their ill." מרפּא for מרפּא, to cause the hands of any one to be relaxed, i.e., to make him dispirited; cf. Ezr 4:4; Isa 35:3. דּרשׁ with ל htiw , as <reference osisRef="Job.10.6">Job 10:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.12.30">Deu 12:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.19">1Ch 22:19</reference>, etc., elsewhere with the accusatival את; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.29.7">Jer 29:7</reference> <hi type="italic">et passim</hi>. On this point cf. Jer 29:7. The allegation which the princes made against Jeremiah was possibly correct. The constancy with which Jeremiah declared that resistance was useless, since, in accordance with the divine decree, Jerusalem was to be taken and burnt by the Chaldeans, could not but make the soldiers and the people unwilling any longer to sacrifice their lives in defending the city. Nevertheless the complaint was unjust, because Jeremiah was not expressing his own personal opinion, but was declaring the word of the Lord, and that, too, not from any want of patriotism or through personal cowardice, but in the conviction, derived from the divine revelation, that it was only by voluntary submission that the fate of the besieged could be mitigated; hence he acted from a deep feeling of love to the people, and in order to avert complete destruction from them. The courage of the people which he sought to weaken was not a heroic courage founded on genuine trust in God, but carnal obstinacy, which could not but lead to ruin.
entries.7da416f56ac5ce4f6570d0017c96e3e7e98b40a6: <reference osisRef="Jer.38.5">Jer 38:5</reference> <hi type="italic">The king said, "Behold, he is in your hand, for the king can do nothing alongside of you."</hi> This reply indicates not merely the weakness and powerlessness of the king against his princes, but also his inward aversion to the testimony of the man of God. "That he would like to save him, just as he afterwards does (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.10">Jer 38:10</reference>)," is not implied in what he says, with which he delivers up the prophet to the spite of his enemies. Though the princes had at once put Jeremiah to death, the king would not even have been able to reproach them. The want of courage vigorously to oppose the demand of the princes did not spring from any kindly feeling towards the prophet, but partly from moral weakness of character, partly from inward repugnance to the word of God proclaimed by Jeremiah. On the construction אין וּיכל instead of the participle from יכול, which does not occur, cf. Ewald, §321, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. אתכם is certainly in form an accusative; but it cannot be such, since דּבר follows as the accusative: it is therefore either to be pointed אתּכם or to be considered as standing for it, just as אותך often occurs for אתּך, "with," i.e., "along with you."
entries.c783057d5276fbf3608e3ddb0ece507ab45dfadd: <reference osisRef="Jer.38.6">Jer 38:6</reference> <div eID="gen14295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14296" type="x-p"/> The princes (שׂרים) now cast Jeremiah into the pit of the king’s son (בּן־מלך, see on <reference osisRef="Jer.36.26">Jer 36:26</reference>) Malchiah, which was in the court of the prison, letting him down with ropes into the pit, in which there was no water, but mud; into this Jeremiah sank. The act is first mentioned in a general way in the words, "they cast him into the pit;" then the mode of proceeding is particularized in the words, "and they let him down," etc. On the expression הבּור מלכּיּהוּ, "the pit of Malchiah," cf. Ewald, §290, <hi type="italic">d</hi>: the article stands here before the <hi type="italic">nomen regens</hi>, because the <hi type="italic">nomen rectum</hi>, from being a proper name, cannot take it; and yet the pit must be pointed out as one well known and definite. That it was very deep, and that Jeremiah must have perished in it if he were not soon taken out again, is evident from the very fact that they were obliged to use ropes in letting him down, and still more so from the trouble caused in pulling him out (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.10-Jer.38.12">Jer 38:10-12</reference>). That the princes did not at once put the prophet to death with the sword was not owing to any feeling of respect for the king, because the latter had not pronounced sentence of death on him, but because they sought to put the prophet to a final death, and yet at the same time wished to silence the voice of conscience with the excuse that they had not shed his blood.
entries.1b00b8820e68e022e1c1356e333a7ce88d3e2ef4: <reference osisRef="Jer.38.7-Jer.38.9">Jer 38:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen14296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14297" type="x-p"/> The deliverance of Jeremiah. Ebedmelech the Cushite, a eunuch, heard of what had happened to Jeremiah. אישׁ סריס .haimer signifies a eunuch: the אישׁ shows that סריס is here to be taken in its proper meaning, not in the metaphorical sense of an officer of the court. Since the king had many wives (Jer 38:22.), the presence of a eunuch at the court, as overseer of the harem, cannot seem strange. The law of Moses, indeed, prohibited castration (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.2">Deu 23:2</reference>); but the man was a foreigner, and had been taken by the king into his service as one castrated. עבד מלך is a proper name (otherwise it must have been written המּלך); the name is a genuine Hebrew one, and probably may have been assumed when the man entered the service of Zedekiah. - On hearing of what had occurred, the Ethiopian went to the king, who was sitting in the gate of Benjamin, on the north wall of the city, which was probably the point most threatened by the besiegers, and said to him, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.9">Jer 38:9</reference>, <hi type="italic">"My lord, O king, these men have acted wickedly in all that they have done to Jeremiah the prophet, whom they have cast into the pit; and he is dying of hunger on the spot, for there is no more bread in the city."</hi> הרעוּ את־א, lit.,: "they have done wickedly what they have done." ויּמת cannot be translated, "and he died on the spot," for Ebedmelech wishes to save him before he dies of hunger. But neither does it stand for וימת, "so that he must die." The imperfect with Vav consecutive expresses the consequence of a preceding act, and usually stands in the narrative as a historic tense; but it may also declare what necessarily follows or will follow from what precedes; cf. Ewald, §342, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. Thus ויּמת stands here in the sense, "and so he is dying," i.e., "he must die of hunger." תּחתּיו, "on his spot," i.e., on the place where he is; cf. 2Sa 2:23. The reason, "for there is no longer any bread (הלחם with the article, the necessary bread) in the city," is not to be taken in the exact sense of the words, but merely expresses the greatest deficiency in provisions. As long as Jeremiah was in the court of the prison, he received, like the officers of the court, at the king’s order, his ration of bread every day (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.21">Jer 37:21</reference>). But after he had been cast into the pit, that royal ordinance no longer applied to him, so that he was given over to the tender mercies of others, from whom, in the prevailing scarcity of bread, he had not much to hope for.
entries.e82fbfb8bbdb05f974ca4b252efe0d2017927dd3: <reference osisRef="Jer.38.10">Jer 38:10</reference> <hi type="italic">Then the king commanded the Ethiopian, "Take hence thirty men in thine hand, and bring up Jeremiah out of the pit before he dies."</hi> בידך, "in thine hand," i.e., under your direction; cf. Num 31:49. The number thirty has been found too great; and Ewald, Hitzig, and Graf would read שׁלשׁה, because the syntax requires the singular אישׁ after שׁלשׁים, and because at that time, when the fighting men had already decreased in number (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.4">Jer 38:4</reference>), thirty men could not be sent away from a post in danger without difficulty. These two arguments are quite invalid. The syntax does not demand אישׁ; for with the tens (20-90) the noun frequently follows in the plural as well as in the singular, if the number precede; cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.20">2Sa 3:20</reference>; 2Ki 2:16, etc.; see also Gesenius’ <hi type="italic">Grammar</hi>, §120, 2. The other argument is based on arbitrary hypotheses; for the passage neither speaks of fighting men, nor states that they would be taken from a post in danger. Ebedmelech was to take thirty men, not because they would all be required for drawing out the prophet, but for making surer work in effecting the deliverance of the prophet, against all possible attempts on the part of the princes or of the populace to prevent them.
entries.e18b3f094bff3a4c1493b8f82c98562d355fd18c: <reference osisRef="Jer.38.11-Jer.38.13">Jer 38:11-13</reference> <hi type="italic">Ebedmelech took the men at his hand, went into the king’s house under the treasury, and took thence rags of torn and of worn-out garments, and let them down on ropes to Jeremiah into the pit, and said to him, "Put, I pray thee, the rages of the torn and cast-off clothes under thine arm-pits under the ropes."</hi> <hi type="italic">Jeremiah did so, and then they drew him out of the pit by the ropes</hi>. תּחת is a room under the treasury. בּלוי, in <reference osisRef="Jer.38.12">Jer 38:12</reference> בּלואים, from בּלה, to be worn away (of clothes), are rags. סחבות (from סחב, to drag, drag about, tear to pieces) are torn pieces of clothing. מלחים, worn-out garments, from מלח, in Niphal, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.6">Isa 51:6</reference>, to vanish, dissolve away. The article at הסּחבות is expunged from the <hi type="italic">Qeri</hi> for sake of uniformity, because it is not found with מלחים; but it may as well be allowed to stand as be removed. אצּילות ידים, properly the roots of the hands, are not the knuckles of the hand, but the shoulders of the arms. מתּחת לחבלים, under the ropes; i.e., the rags were to serve as pads to the ropes which were to be placed under the arm-pits, to prevent the ropes from cutting the flesh. When Jeremiah had been drawn out in this way from the deep pit of mire, he remained in the court of the prison.
entries.144deeee36b6d763fbabbe8899b48343406097ed: <reference osisRef="Jer.38.14-Jer.38.16">Jer 38:14-16</reference> <hi type="italic">Conversation between the king and the prophet.</hi> - Jer 38:14. King Zedekiah was desirous of once more hearing a message of God from the prophet, and for this object had him brought into the third entrance in the house of the Lord. Nothing further is known about the situation and the nature of this entrance; possibly it led from the palace to the temple, and seems to have been an enclosed space, for the king could carry on a private conversation there with the prophet. The king said to him, "I ask you about a matter, do not conceal anything from me." He meant a message from God regarding the final issue of the siege, cf. Jer 37:7. Jeremiah, knowing the aversion of the king to the truth, replies, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.15">Jer 38:15</reference> : <hi type="italic">"If I tell thee [sc. the word of the Lord], wilt thou not assuredly kill me? And if I were to give thee advice, thou wouldst not listen to me."</hi> Jer 38:16. Then the king sware to him secretly, "As Jahveh liveth, who hath made us this soul, I shall certainly not kill thee, nor deliver thee into the hand of these men who seek thy life." את אשׁר, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.27.8">Jer 27:8</reference>, properly means, "with regard to Him who has created us." The <hi type="italic">Qeri</hi> expunges את. "These men" are the princes mentioned in Jer 38:1.
entries.0424b35b065cebc066d286338f62fd2b8270007c: <reference osisRef="Jer.38.17-Jer.38.18">Jer 38:17-18</reference> <hi type="italic">After this solemn asseveration of the king, Jeremiah said to him, "Thus saith Jahveh, the God of hosts, the God of Israel: If thou wilt assuredly go out to the princes of the king of Babylon  [i.e., wilt surrender thyself to them, cf. 2Ki 18:31; 2Ki 24:12], then thy soul shall live, and this city shall not be burned with fire, and thou and thy house shall live. But if thou dost not go out to the princes of the king of Babylon, then this city will be given into the hand of the Chaldeans, and they shall burn it with fire, and thou shalt not escape out of their hand."</hi> The word of God is the same that Jeremiah had already repeatedly announced to the king, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.34.2-Jer.34.5">Jer 34:2-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.4">Jer 32:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.21.4">Jer 21:4</reference>-10. The princes (chiefs, generals) of the king of Babylon are named, because they commanded the besieging army (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.3">Jer 39:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.39.13">Jer 39:13</reference>); Nebuchadnezzar himself had his headquarters at Riblah, Jer 39:5.
entries.ab27762806cfd6405f73cce666284734b914d61d: <reference osisRef="Jer.38.19-Jer.38.23">Jer 38:19-23</reference> <div eID="gen14297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14298" type="x-p"/> Against the advice that he should save his life by surrendering to the Chaldeans, Zedekiah suggests the consideration, "I am afraid of the Jews, who have deserted [נפל אל as in Jer 37:13] to the Chaldeans, lest they give me into their hands and maltreat me." התעלּל בּ, <hi type="italic">illudere alicui</hi>, to abuse any one by mockery or ill-treatment; cf. Num 22:29; <reference osisRef="1Chr.10.4">1Ch 10:4</reference>, etc. Jeremiah replies, Jer 38:20., <hi type="italic">"They will not give thee up. Yet, pray, listen to the voice of Jahveh, in that which I say to thee, that it may be well with thee, and that thy soul may live. </hi> Jer 38:21. <hi type="italic">But if thou dost refuse to go out i.e., to surrender thyself to the Chaldeans, this is the word which the Lord hath shown me has revealed to me: </hi> Jer 38:22. <hi type="italic">Behold, all the women that are left in the house of the king of Judah shall be brought out to the princes of the king of Babylon, and those [women] shall say, Thy friends have misled thee and have overcome thee; thy feet are sunk in the mud, they have turned away back. </hi> Jer 38:23. <hi type="italic">And all thy wives and thy children shall they bring out to the Chaldeans, and thou shalt not escape out of their hand; for thou shalt be seized by the hand of the king of Babylon, and thou shalt burn this city with fire."</hi> - After Jeremiah had once more assured the king that he would save his life by voluntary surrender, he announces to him that, on the other alternative, instead of his becoming the sport of the deserters, the women of his harem would be insulted. The women who remain in the king’s house, as distinguished from "thy wives" (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.23">Jer 38:23</reference>), are the women of the royal harem, the wives of former kings, who remain in the harem as the concubines of the reigning king. These are to be brought out to the generals of the Chaldean king, and to sing a satire on him, to this effect: "Thy friends have misled thee, and overpowered thee," etc. The first sentence of this song is from Oba 1:7, where השּׁיאוּך ere stands instead of הסּיתוּך. The friends (אנשׁי שׁלמך, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.20.10">Jer 20:10</reference>) are his great men and his false prophets. Through their counsels, these have led him astray, and brought him into a bog, in which his feet stick fast, and then they have gone back; i.e., instead of helping him out, they have deserted him, leaving him sticking in the bog. The expression is figurative, and the meaning of the figure is plain (רגלך is plural). בּץ, ἁπ λεγ.., is equivalent to בּצּה, a bog, Job 8:11. Moreover, the wives and children of Zedekiah are to fall into the hand of the Chaldeans. מוצאים, the participle, is used instead of the finite tense to express the notion of indefinite personality: "they bring them out." תּתּפשׂ בּיד ".tuo meht gnirb , properly, "to be seized in the hand," is a pregnant construction for, "to fall into the hand and be held fast by it." "Thou shalt burn this city," i.e., bring the blame of burning it upon thyself. Ewald, Hitzig, and Graf, following the lxx, Syr., and Chald., would change תּשׂרף into תּשּׂרף, but needlessly.
entries.35c49d2d8c51ee0872df582d841c353f35262026: <reference osisRef="Jer.38.24-Jer.38.26">Jer 38:24-26</reference> <div eID="gen14298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14299" type="x-p"/> From the king’s weakness of character, and his dependence on his evil counsellors, neither could this interview have any result. Partly from want of firmness, but chiefly from fear of the reproaches of his princes, he did not venture to surrender himself and the city to the Chaldeans. Hence he did not wish that his interview with the prophet should be known, partly for the purpose of sparing himself reproaches from the princes, partly also, perhaps, not to expose the prophet to further persecutions on the part of the great men. Accordingly, he dismissed Jeremiah with this instruction: "Let no man know of these words, lest thou die." But if the princes should learn that the king had been speaking with him, and asked him, "Tell us, now, what thou hast said to the king, do not hide it from us, and we will not kill thee; and what did the king say to thee?" then he was to say to them, "I presented my supplication before the king, that he would not send me back to the house of Jonathan, to die there."
