entries.a9c3a1c11dc43243f674377246c885513046b80f: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.38.25" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jer.38.25" sID="gen63529" type="section"/> <div sID="gen63530" type="x-p"/>Here again Zedekiah shews his anxiety, lest Jeremiah should be apprehended, were the princes unexpectedly to assail him; for he might in this respect have stumbled, though admonished. Then the king intimated to him what to answer, in case the counselors came to him and made inquiry respecting their intercourse. He then advised him simply to say, that he <hi type="italic">entreated </hi>him not to send him back to the filthy pit, where he almost perished. The miserable servitude of the king appears now still evident; for he feared his own counselors, lest they should revolt from him. he might easily have made a spontaneous surrender of himself, but he dared not, lest he should be killed by them in a tumult; and yet, on the other hand, he feared lest the princes should despise him, and so redeem themselves by the sacrifice of his life.<div eID="gen63530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen63531" type="x-p"/>We see in what straits he was, but God rendered to him a just recompense for his obstinacy. It was indeed a miserable thing to hear that the king’ was thus oppressed on every side, but the cause of all this ought ever to be borne in mind; which was, that he had despised God and his Prophet. He then deserved to be in this state of anxiety, to fear death on every side, and not to be able to extricate himself from those cares and perplexities which tormented him.<div eID="gen63531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen63532" type="x-p"/>Let us then learn to cast all our cares on God, so that our life may be safe, and that we may have calm and tranquil minds: otherwise what is written in the Law must necessarily happen to us,<div eID="gen63532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen63533" type="x-p"/>“Our life will hang on a thread, so that we shall say in the morning, Who will give us to see the evening? and in the evening, How can we live to the morning?” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.66 Bible:Deut.28.67">Deuteronomy 28:66, 67</reference>)<div eID="gen63533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen63534" type="x-p"/>Lest then the same thing happen to us as to this miserable king, let us learn to re-cumb on God, for this is the only way to obtain peace.<div eID="gen63534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen63535" type="x-p"/>For though Zedekiah set before Jeremiah the danger which he might bring on himself, if he confessed what took place between them, he yet had a regard no doubt to his own safety, for his care for the Prophet was not very great. <hi type="italic">If, then, </hi>he says, <hi type="italic">the princes will hear that I have spoken to him, etc</hi>. We see here, that as kings very curiously inquire into the sayings and actions of all, so they in their turn are exposed to innumerable spies, who observe all their secret proceedings. Zedekiah, as we have already seen, left his palace, sought some secret place, and at the third entrance called to him Jeremiah. This place might be deemed in some measure secret, yet he knew that he was observed even by his own servants.<div eID="gen63535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen63536" type="x-p"/>Thus kings, while they seek immoderate splendor, renounce the main good, which ought to be preferred to all other things. For it is commonly said that liberty is an invaluable gift, and it is very true: but were we to seek for liberty among mankind, we should by no means find it in courts; for all there are slaves, and slavery begins with the most elevated. Kings, then, while they thus seek from their height to look down on all mankind, are placed, as it were, in a theater, and the eyes of all turn to them, so that no liberty remains for them; and they who hang on their favor are also in constant fear. This, then, ought to be noticed by us; for there is no one who does not seek splendor; but yet we know how anxious is the life of princes. Their external appearance is indeed very flattering; but we do not see what inward torments harass them. When, therefore, it is said of Zedekiah, that he could not have a secret conference, it hence appears that kings are by no means free.<div eID="gen63536" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.38.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen63529" osisID="Jer.38.25" type="section"/>
entries.259dff7c3a19856e3ab50c4f891ec29aca4fbb27:
He says, “Though they promise thee impunity, trust them not.” Zedekiah feared lest the Prophet should be too credulous, and should freely relate to the counselors what he had said. But he no doubt had reflected on the fact, that the Prophet had already announced the destruction of the city. He then could have hardly hoped for the silence which he required. Hence then it was, that he so earnestly bid him to be careful; and though the counselors should promise that there would be no danger to him, he yet bade him to be silent. Say to them, he said, I humbly prayed the king not to send me back to the house of Jonathan, that I might not die there It was not indeed a falsehood, but this evasion cannot be wholly excused. The Prophet justly feared, and, as we have before seen, he was perplexed and anxious, for that prison was horrible, and it would have been better at once to die than to have been thus buried alive in the earth. But it is certain that he did not come to the king for this purpose, for he had been sent for. Though, then, the Prophet did not expressly or in so many words say what was false, yet it was a kind of falsehood; and what follows, in reference to himself, cannot be excused.
Jeremiah 38:27
27. Then came all the princes unto Jeremiah, and asked him: and he told them according to all these words that the king had commanded. So they left off speaking with him; for the matter was not perceived.
27. Et venerunt cuncti proceres ad Jeremiam, et interrogarunt ipsum; et annuntiavit illis (hoc est, narravit illis) secundum sermones istos, quemadmodum praeceperat rex, et siluerunt ab eo, quia sermo non fuit auditus.
entries.c4c47d2d1c9ede7beb4c5683dfaf602e25afac8c:
Here, indeed, the Prophet confesses that he did as the king had commanded him; but he does not commend what he had done. There is no doubt but that on the one hand he placed before his eyes the timidity of the king, who, being forgetful of plain dealing, slavishly feared his own counselors; and that., on the other hand, he manifested that he was not sufficiently discreet, for when the princes came, even if he wished not to deceive them, he yet concealed the main thing, and said that he went to the king to pray for his own life, which was not true. Though then what he said was in part true, that he prayed not. to be sent back to prison, yet he could not by this evasion be wholly exempted from blame.
In short, we see that even God’s servants have sometimes spoken evasively, when oppressed with extreme fear; and thus we are reminded to seek of God magnanimity of mind and resolute firmness; for he alone can strengthen and sustain us when we are terrified by any fear of danger.
He says, that he did as the king had commanded him; but he ought rather to have hearkened to God’s word, in which simplicity is enjoined. It is also said, that the princes were silent, that is, departed in silence; for no one had been a witness to the conference, and the matter had not spread farther; for the king was silent through fear, and the Prophet also had not made known the secret interview. Hence it was that the princes departed, and thought that the matter was as represented. In short, Jeremiah intimates that they were deceived by this pretext. It follows at last, —
Jeremiah 38:28
28. So Jeremiah abode in the court of the prison until the day that Jerusalem was taken: and he was there when Jerusalem was taken.
28. Et habitavit Jeremias in atrio custodiae, usque ad diem quo capta fuit Jerusalem; et accidit secundum quod capta fuit Jerusalem.
entries.cc39691f408f37beb97f6a866fb06dda79ea0076:
Some render the last words simply thus, “And it happened that Jerusalem was taken;” and others, “It happened accordingly that Jerusalem was taken;” but this seems unnatural. Others take the relative as a demonstrative pronoun, and of this I approve, “For it happened that according to this Jerusalem was taken.”
He first says that he dwelt in the court of the prison. It hence appears that he was not even then at liberty; for though the king wished him to be free, yet he dared not to release him. This is one thing. Then he says, that he was there until the day the city was taken We shall hereafter see that he was saved by the king’s command, and was brought out of prison. He was, then, until that day in the court of the prison, as though he had said, that he was a prisoner until the king was taken prisoner, together with his counselors, and also until the day the whole city was taken. And here we may see, as in a vivid form, the wonderful judgment of God. As long as the Jews boasted that they offered sacrifices to God, they kept Jeremiah shut up in prison, so that he was not a free man until the king was taken, the city perished, and almost all were driven into exile. I have no doubt but that he added the following by way of explanation, And it happened that according to this Jerusalem was taken; that is, he reminds readers in these words, that he had not been a false Prophet, but a true and faithful witness as to God’s judgment, for all his prophecies were verified by the event.
These words are left out in the Sept. and the Syriac. The Vulgate, and the Targum. give this version, “And it came to pass that Jerusalem was taken;” which seems not in this connection to have any meaning. Some connect them with the following chapter, but improperly. Our version, followed by Blayney, gives the best sense, “And he was there (that is, in the court of the prison) when Jerusalem was taken:“ He was there not only to the day or time of its capture, but during that time. This was added to shew that he was not released by the Jews, but by those who took the city. — Ed.
He then says that the city was taken, not by chance, but because God had so declared. He now begins to narrate historically the destruction and the burning of the city. He therefore says, —
CHAPTER 39
Jeremiah 39:1-2
1. In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, came Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon and all his army against Jerusalem, and they besieged it.
1. Anno nono Zedechiae regis Jehudah, mense decimo venit Nebuchadnezer rex Babylonis et totus exercitus ejus Jerosolymam, et obsiderunt eam.
2 And in the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, the ninth day of the month, the city was broken up.
2. In undecimo anno Zedechiae, mense quarto, nona mensis, disrupta fuit urbs.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="38" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. XXXVIII.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 THen Shephatiah the son of Mattan, and Gedaliah the son of Pashur, and Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashur the son of Malchiah, heard the words that Jeremiah had spoken to all the people, saying <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Here are four of the great men Councellors, or great offi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cers to <ns0:hi>Zedekiah</ns0:hi> named, of whom we have no further mention in holy Writ, nor are they worthy of much inquiry after; <ns0:hi>Ie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />remiah</ns0:hi> being now removed into a little freer air, where his friends, or such as had a desire to see him, came to him, and it is very likely were inquisitive to know what God would do with the City, he could not but tell them what he knew of the mind of God in the case, and advise them the best he could. Some of them go to these Princes, and inform them of what they had heard from the Prophet.</ns0:note>,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 Thus saith the LORD, He that remaineth in this City shall dye by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence, but he that goeth forth to the Chaldeans shall live: for he shall have his life for a prey, and shall live <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">As to what is <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 3. it is no more then had for some time been the constant tenour of this Prophets prophesies. The crime seemeth to lye in this, that in such a time of extream danger, he should repeat this prophesie, and also advise the people to leave the City, and shift for themselves, by going out to the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans,</ns0:hi> telling them that if they did so, though the City would be lost, and their Estates in it lost, yet they should save their lives, which words might incourage many of low and cowardly spirits to desert their posts; which indeed had been crime sufficient in an ordinary time, and under ordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nary circumstances, but was no crime, now that God had re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vealed his will to the King, Princes and people, that the City should be lost, there lay now no further duty upon any to con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tribute to its defence, but they were obliged to make as good provisions for themselves as they could; but these wicked Princes believed no such thing, therefore they make this a great charge.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 Thus faith the LORD, This city shall surely be given into the hand of the king of Babylons army, which shall take it.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 Therefore the princes said unto the king, We beseech thee let this man be put to death: for thus he weakneth the hands of the men of war that remain in this city, and the hands of all the people, in speaking such words unto them: for this man seeketh not the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>Peace.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> welfare of this people, but the hurt <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The Prophet now seemeth under sad circumstances, the Princes seek his life, though for delivering no other doctrine then he had been preaching for 20 years, their pretence was; 1. His discouraging and weakening the military part of the City, letting them know that they laboured in vain, for the City was not defensible. This they interpret a seeking not the welfare of the people, but their hurt, though indeed their wel<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fare was that alone which he sought, knowing that there was no other way for any of them to save their lives, but by submit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ting to the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans,</ns0:hi> though the great men (being persons God had determined to ruine) would not believe it, and will have the welfare and hurt of the place determined by their opinions</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 Then Zedekiah the king said, Behold, he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in your hand <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">That is in your power, either by the Established Law a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst false Prophets, or else I yield up my power to you, I surrender him into your hands; but neither of these seemeth very probable, for here is no mention of the sitting of the <ns0:hi>San<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hedrim</ns0:hi> to judge him as a false Prophet, nor of any judicial pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceedings of that Nature: And it should seem by <ns0:hi>Zedekiahs</ns0:hi> re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieving of him soon after from the dungeon, into which they threw him, that he had not surrendred <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> so into their hands, but he reserved to himself a superintendency upon them to correct their too severe dealings with him. The meaning seems rather to be, if you will do any such thing, I shall not op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pose you, but I will not be the Author of it.</ns0:note>, for the king <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> not <ns0:hi>he that</ns0:hi> can do <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> thing against you <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">I see I am as it were no King, I can do nothing against you, you will do what you please. I incline to this sense from the consideration of the favour shewed him by <ns0:hi>Zedekiah,</ns0:hi> both before, and after this.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 Then took they Jeremiah, and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah the son of <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>of the King</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> Hamme<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lech that <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> in the court of the prison <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">A place much of the same nature with that of which we read, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 37.16. but in another prison.</ns0:note>: and they let down Jeremiah with cords <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">It should seem there was no passage into it by stairs, so as they were forced to let him down with cords.</ns0:note>. And in the dungeon <ns0:hi>there was</ns0:hi> no water but mire, so Je<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />remiah sank in the mire <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">And in the bottom was nothing but mire, into which the Prophet sank, in respect of which cir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cumstances, it was a much worse place then the dungeon in the prison, in <ns0:hi>Jonathans</ns0:hi> house appeared to be, though <ns0:hi>Jeremiah</ns0:hi> feared that he should dye there. It is probable these Princes thrust him into this place, designing he should dye in this hole a miserable death, but God otherwise provided for him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 ¶ Now when <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 39.16.</ns0:note> Ebed-melech the Ethiopi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />an <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Ebedmelech</ns0:hi> was unquestionably the name of the person, though some interpret it appellatively <ns0:hi>a servant of the King,</ns0:hi> it is particularly noted that he was an <ns0:hi>Ethiopian</ns0:hi> or a <ns0:hi>C<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>shite,</ns0:hi> to let us know that this Prophet of the Lord sound more kindness from a stranger, that was a Native Heathen, then from his own coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />trymen.</ns0:note>, one of the eunuchs which was in the kings house <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Princes were wont to keep <ns0:hi>Eunuchs</ns0:hi> in their houses in those countries, 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 9.32. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 1.9. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 8.27. it should seem the Princes had privately put <ns0:hi>Jeremiah</ns0:hi> into this miserable place, but yet the noise of it came to <ns0:hi>Ebedmelechs</ns0:hi> ear, who was attending in the Court.</ns0:note>, heard that they had put Jeremiah in the dungeon <ns0:hi>i,</ns0:hi> (the king then sitting in the gate of Benjamin) <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The Gates of the City were places where Princes were wont to sit to execute justice, and to receive Petitions, and give answers, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 19.8. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>1.23. &c.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:50" />8 Ebed-melech went forth out of the kings house, and spake to the king, saying,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they have done to Jeremiah the pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phet, whom they have cast into the dungeon, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e will dye.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> he is like to dye for hunger in the place where he is, for <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> no more bread in the city <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">The courage of this good <ns0:hi>E<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>nuch</ns0:hi> was very remarkable, he did not stay till the King came in, but went to the King, as he was sitting in the <ns0:hi>gate of Benjamin,</ns0:hi> administring justice, or receiving and answering petitions, where doubtless he was not alone, and probably was attended there, by some of those Princes, who had thrown <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> into this miserable place: <ns0:hi>Ebedmelech</ns0:hi> was not afraid of them, but openly complains of their cruelty to the King, and tells him that <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> would be starved to death, those that were alive in the City could not long subsist, for the stores were almost all spent, and though the King had appointed the Prophet an allowance, yet being in such an hole, and there being so little bread left in the City, it was not likely there would be much care taken of him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Then the king commanded Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, saying, Take from hence thirty men <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>in thi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> hand.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> with thee, and take up Jeremiah the pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phet out of the dungeon before he die <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">There are several guesses why the King commandeth <ns0:hi>E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bedmelech</ns0:hi> to take <ns0:hi>thirty men</ns0:hi> for the doing of that for which three or four were sufficient. I think they judge best, who think it was to guard him against any opposition. Things were now in a great disorder, the City being upon the matter taken, and the King himself was much in the Government of his Princes, and as may easily be judged by what went before, and what we shall hereafter meet with, could not rule them, but was in some fear of them, and he did not know but some of the most boi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sterous of them, might oppose the execution of this command of his. This King in his whole story seemeth to have been of a much better humour then his predecessors, and to have had a kindness for the Prophet, though he suffered himself to be miserably over-ruled by his Courtiers, who were of a much fiercer temper, and worse affected to the Prophet.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 So Ebed-melech took the men with him, and went into the house of the king under the treasury, and took thence old cast clouts, and old rotten rags, and let them down by cords in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to the dungeon to Jeremiah.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 And Ebed-melech the Ethiopian said unto Jeremiah, Put now <ns0:hi>these</ns0:hi> old cast clouts, and rot<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ten rags under thine arm holes, under the cords. And Jeremiah did so.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 So they drew up Jeremiah with cords, and took him up out of the dungeon, And Jeremiah re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mained in the court of the prison <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The sense of these verses is obvious. <ns0:hi>Ebedmelech</ns0:hi> having received a commission from the King presently puts it in exe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cution, only because the dungeon was deep, and full of rain, and the Prophet possibly not over well cloathed, he prudently takes some old clouts, and rags, and lets them down with cords, that <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> to prevent the galling and macerating his flesh, might put them under the cords, by which they drew him up: Thus he was restored to the <ns0:hi>Court of the Prison,</ns0:hi> where he was before this suggestion of the Princes, and where he did abide until the City was taken. The rest of the Chapter is spent in a private conference betwixt King <ns0:hi>Zedekiah</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Prophet,</ns0:hi> after he was restored to the <ns0:hi>Court of the Prison.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 ¶ Then Zedekiah the king sent, and took Jeremiah the prophet unto him into the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or <ns0:hi>principal.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> third entry that <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in the house of the LORD <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Some think that this were better Translated, that is, <ns0:hi>near the house of the Lord,</ns0:hi> and that this <ns0:hi>third entry</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>principal entry,</ns0:hi> was that <ns0:hi>ascent out of the Kings house</ns0:hi> into the Temple, mentioned 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 10.5. which was one of the things the <ns0:hi>Queen of Sheba admired,</ns0:hi> for it is hardly probable, that <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> being in a pri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son within the compass of the Kings house, the King should es<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pecially at such a time go out of his house to so publick a place as the Temple, for a private conference with the Prophet.</ns0:note>; And the king said unto Jeremiah, I will ask thee a thing: hide nothing from me <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The King desires him faithfully to tell him what he knew in a business he should inquire of him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 Then Jeremiah said unto Zedekiah, If I de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clare <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> unto thee, wilt thou not surely put me to death <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">

We must imagine <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> at this time under no divine command, to reveal his will in this case unto the King.</ns0:note>? and if I give thee counsel, wilt thou not hearken unto me <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">

Zedekiah</ns0:hi> had often been advised by the Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phet, but would never take his advice, and the Prophet knew it would be the same case still, that the King would be over<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ruled by a corrupt Court, and his own aversion, to change his state, as a King, for the state of a prisoner.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 So Zedekiah the king sware secretly unto Jeremiah, saying, <ns0:hi>As</ns0:hi> the LORD liveth, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 57.16.</ns0:note> that made us this soul, I will not put thee to death, neither will I give thee into the hand of these men that seek thy life <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Zedekiah</ns0:hi> saith nothing to the latter part of <ns0:hi>Ieremiahs</ns0:hi> speech, promising nothing as to his hearing and obeying his counsel: As to the former he gives him the security of his Oath, that he would neither himself slay him, by giving any immediate com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mand from himself, nor surrender him up into the hands of those malitious Princes, who he perceived sought his life. The form of his Oath is what was usual, <ns0:hi>as the Lord liveth,</ns0:hi> with an addition, the Lord that gave me my life, <ns0:hi>if I put thee to death,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>if I deliver thee,</ns0:hi> which form carrieth with it a concealed imprecation. <ns0:hi>Let the Lord do so to me,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>more also,</ns0:hi> or let the Lord that gave me this soul take it from me, if I do either of these things. Thus he secures <ns0:hi>Jeremiah,</ns0:hi> as to any hard measure for his telling him the truth, though it should be what might be interpreted a capital crime to publish.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 Then said Jeremiah unto Zedekiah, Thus saith the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel, if thou wilt assuredly go forth unto the king of Babylons princes, then thy soul shall live <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">That is, thou shalt live.</ns0:note>, and this city shall not be burnt with fire, and thou shalt live, and thine house <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">And thou shalt save the City from being burned with fire, and thy Wives and Children from death. God did certainly know that <ns0:hi>Zedekiah</ns0:hi> would not do this, though it was in his power to do it, yet he doth not judge it vain for him to exhort him to do it, and to annex such a promise; for thereby he was left inexcusable, in his not saving the City, and his Relations lives.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 But if thou wilt not go forth to the king of Babylons princes, then shall this city be given into the hand of the Chaldeans, and they shall burn it with fire, and thou shalt not escape out of their hand <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">As he before had used exhortations and promises, so here he useth threatnings to perswade him to that which indeed was in his power to do, but God infallibly knew that he would not do. The end of God in which could be no other then to leave him without excuse, in not obeying what God commanded.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 And Zedekiah the king said unto Jeremiah, I am afraid of the Jews, that are fallen to the Chaldeans, lest they deliver me into their hand, and they mock me <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">But if <ns0:hi>Zedekiah</ns0:hi> went out according to the Prophets ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vice, and delivered himself, what needed he to fear his Sub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jects, that had deserted the City, delivering of him? It seems rather therefore to be the sense, lest the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> when I have yielded my self to them, should deliver me into the hands of those <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> which have fallen to them, and they should mock me, so as he seems to be more concerned for his honour then for his own life, and his Families, and the whole City; thus often great persons are more patient of death, then of reproach and dishonour.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 But Jeremiah said, They shall not deliver <ns0:hi>thee</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> shall not do so base an act, but deal with thee as with a Prince.</ns0:note>: Obey, I beseech thee, the voice of the LORD, which I speak unto thee: so it shall be well unto thee, and thy soul shall live.<ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Let not this therefore be a tempta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion to thee, to disobey the command of God, which if thou doest thou shalt live, though not in that splendor in which thou now livest, yet in a much more comfortable state, then thou wilt do if they take the City by storming.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 But if thou refuse to go forth, this <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the word that the LORD hath shewed me:</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 And behold all the women that are left in the king of Judahs house, <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> brought forth to the king of Babylons princes <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Thou that art afraid of the insultings of men that are thy Subjects, shalt fall under the insultings, and taunts of the Wo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />men, either the <ns0:hi>Court Ladies</ns0:hi> who were left when <ns0:hi>Ie<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                  </ns0:note> Thy friends have set thee on, and have prevailed against thee, thy feet are sunk in the mire <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">And tell thee for this thou maist thank thy hearkening to thy Priests, and false Prophets called in the Heb. <ns0:hi>the men of thy peace,</ns0:hi> because they soothed up the King with the promises of peace.</ns0:note>

               <ns0:p n="23">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:50" />23 So they shall bring out all thy wives and thy children to the Chaldeans, and thou shalt not escape out of their hand, but shalt be taken by the hand of the king of Babylon: and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>thou shalt b<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                        </ns0:gap>rn,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> thou shalt cause this city, to be burnt with fire <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">This is no more then what was said before, onely here re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />peated, as an Argument to perswade his Obedience in surrendring himself if not for the Cities sake, yet for his own sake, and for his Childrens sake, for he assures the King that not himself onely but his Wives and Children also would otherwise fall into the hands of the <ns0:hi>Babylonians,</ns0:hi> and their reflections upon him for the Misery he had brought upon them, would be no small aggrava<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of his Affliction.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 ¶ Then said Zedekiah unto Jeremiah, Let no man know of these words, and thou shalt not dye <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">These words sufficiently let us know that <ns0:hi>Zedekiah</ns0:hi> stood in awe of his Courtiers, and we might probably think, that had it not been for them, he would have done better. This is the righteous judgment of God, those that will not sanctifie the Lord of Hosts, and make him their fear, shall fear men whom to fear is much more base and ignoble.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 But if the princes hear that I have talked with thee, and they come unto thee, and say unto thee, Declare unto us now what thou hast said un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to the king, hide it not from us, and we will not put thee to death; also what the king said unto thee <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">It could hardly be imagined that <ns0:hi>Zedekiah</ns0:hi> should have this private discourse with <ns0:hi>Ieremiah,</ns0:hi> but some or other of his Cour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiers would take notice of it, but yet it argues that this poor Prince was in a miserable subjection to them, that he could dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />course with no body, but they must come and inquire what he said.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 Then thou shalt say unto them, I presented my supplication before the king, that he would not cause me to return to Jonathans house to die there <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The king instructs the Prophet in case the Princes should be inquisitive to know what discourse passed betwixt the King and him, to tell them, that he petitioned him that he might be sent no more to the Prison in the house of <ns0:hi>Ionathan,</ns0:hi> of which he com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plained, and petitio<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ed the King to be freed from it, <ns0:hi>chapter</ns0:hi> 37.20.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 Then came all the princes to Jeremiah <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">As the King suspected so it came to pass, the Kings private discourse with the Prophet took wind, and all the Princes then at Court came and inquired of <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> what was the substance of his discourse.</ns0:note>, and asked him <ns0:hi>h,</ns0:hi> and he told them according to all these words that the king had commanded <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> answered them according as the King had directed. A man is not bound in all cases to speak the whole truth, much less to those who have nothing to do to in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quire of us which these Princes had not.</ns0:note>: So they left <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>They were silent from him.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> off speaking with him, for the mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter was not perceived <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">By this means the Princes never knew the matter of this discourse.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 So Jeremiah abode in the court of the prison, until the day that Jerusalem was taken, and he was <ns0:hi>there</ns0:hi> when Jerusalem was taken <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Thus God hath several wayes to hide his people in an evil day, he hid <ns0:hi>Iosiah</ns0:hi> from it in the Grave, he hid <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> in an Ark, <ns0:hi>L<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>t</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Zoar, Ieremy</ns0:hi> in a Prison, which in probability was a safer place for him, than the Land of <ns0:hi>Benjamin,</ns0:hi> whither he would have gone, had not <ns0:hi>Irijah</ns0:hi> stopt him, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 37.12, 13. Conque<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rors have commonly the greatest kindness, for those whom they find under the frowns of the conquered, especially when that which hath made them so hath been something spoken, or done in the favour of the Conquerors.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
